name: Cuneiform
what: Wedges pressed into clay, first for temple accounts at Uruk.
why: One of the two oldest writing systems; used for 15 languages over 3,000 years.

sources.cite: Denise Schmandt-Besserat, Before Writing (1992); Hans Nissen, Peter Damerow and Robert Englund, Archaic Bookkeeping (1993)
Stephen Houston (ed.), The First Writing: Script Invention as History and Process (2004)
Abraham Sachs and Hermann Hunger; John Hunger and Teije de Jong, "Almanac W22340a from Uruk: the latest datable cuneiform tablet", Zeitschrift für Assyriologie 103 (2014)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Egyptian hieroglyphs
what: Pictorial signs for words and consonants.
why: Invented about the same time as cuneiform, probably independently; ancestor of the alphabet.

sources.cite: Günter Dreyer, Umm el-Qaab I: Das prädynastische Königsgrab U-j und seine frühen Schriftzeugnisse (1998)
John Baines, "The earliest Egyptian writing", in The First Writing (ed. Houston, 2004)
Jitse Dijkstra, Philae and the End of Ancient Egyptian Religion (2008)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Proto-Elamite
what: Accounting tablets from Susa and the Iranian plateau.
why: Still undeciphered; died within two centuries.

sources.cite: Jacob Dahl, "Early writing in Iran, a reappraisal", Iran 47 (2009)

name: Linear Elamite
what: Elamite writing on stone and silver vessels.
why: Largely deciphered in 2020 to 2022.

sources.cite: François Desset et al., "The Decipherment of Linear Elamite Writing", Zeitschrift für Assyriologie 112 (2022)

name: Indus script
what: Short sign strings on seals.
why: Undeciphered: no long texts and no bilingual, so the Harappans' language is unknown.

sources.cite: Gregory Possehl, The Indus Civilization (2002); Asko Parpola, Deciphering the Indus Script (1994)

name: Linear A
what: Minoan palace records.
why: Undeciphered; its language (Minoan) is unknown.

sources.cite: Roger Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004)

name: Linear B
what: Adapted from Linear A to write Mycenaean Greek.
why: Deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952: Greek, 600 years before Homer.

sources.cite: John Chadwick, The Decipherment of Linear B (1958)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Proto-Sinaitic
what: Canaanite workers used hieroglyph shapes for the first sound of each word.
why: The first alphabet: the ancestor of almost every alphabet used today.

sources.cite: John Darnell et al., "Two early alphabetic inscriptions from the Wadi el-Hol", Annual of the American Schools of Oriental Research 59 (2005)
Orly Goldwasser, "How the alphabet was born from hieroglyphs", Biblical Archaeology Review 36 (2010)

name: Ugaritic alphabet
what: A 30-letter alphabet made of cuneiform wedges.
why: Shows the alphabet's letter order already fixed by 1400 BCE.

sources.cite: Roger Woodard (ed.), The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages (2004)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Phoenician
what: 22 consonant letters, written right to left.
why: Spread by traders across the Mediterranean; parent of Greek and Aramaic.

sources.cite: Joseph Naveh, Early History of the Alphabet (1982)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Aramaic
what: Script of the Assyrian and Persian empires' clerks.
why: Parent of Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic, Sogdian and probably Brahmi.

sources.cite: Joseph Naveh, Early History of the Alphabet (1982)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Greek alphabet
what: Phoenician letters with vowels added.
why: The first full alphabet with vowels; parent of Latin and Cyrillic.

sources.cite: Barry Powell, Homer and the Origin of the Greek Alphabet (1991); Jeffery, The Local Scripts of Archaic Greece (1990)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Old Persian cuneiform
what: A new script made for Darius's inscriptions.
why: The Behistun trilingual was the key to deciphering cuneiform.

sources.cite: Rüdiger Schmitt, The Bisitun Inscriptions of Darius the Great: Old Persian Text (1991)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Etruscan alphabet
what: Borrowed from Euboean Greek colonists at Cumae.
why: The bridge from Greek to Latin letters.

sources.cite: Giuliano and Larissa Bonfante, The Etruscan Language: An Introduction (2nd ed., 2002)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Latin alphabet
what: Adapted from Etruscan.
why: Now the most used script on Earth, spread by Rome, the Church and colonial empires.

sources.cite: Peter Daniels and William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Ancient South Arabian
what: Script of Saba and the incense kingdoms.
why: Parent of the Ethiopic script.

sources.cite: Michael Macdonald, "Ancient Arabia and the written word", in The Development of Arabic as a Written Language (2010)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Ge'ez (Ethiopic)
what: Vowels marked on each consonant from about 350 CE.
why: Still writes Amharic and Tigrinya.

sources.cite: Peter Daniels and William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Brahmi
what: Script of Ashoka's edicts.
why: Ancestor of Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil, Tibetan, Thai, Khmer and Javanese scripts. Its Aramaic origin is the majority view, not proven.

sources.cite: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (1998)
Harry Falk, Schrift im alten Indien (1993)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Kharosthi
what: Right-to-left Indian script from Aramaic.
why: Wrote the oldest Buddhist manuscripts (Gandharan scrolls).

sources.cite: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (1998)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Devanagari
what: Grew out of Brahmi through Gupta and Nagari.
why: Writes Hindi, Marathi, Nepali and Sanskrit.

sources.cite: Richard Salomon, Indian Epigraphy (1998)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Tibetan
what: Made from a north Indian Gupta script under Songtsen Gampo.
why: Carried Buddhist texts across Tibet and Mongolia.

sources.cite: Peter Daniels and William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Khmer
what: Oldest dated Khmer inscription is from 611.
why: Parent of the Thai and Lao scripts.

sources.cite: Peter Daniels and William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Thai
what: Traditionally credited to King Ram Khamhaeng in 1283; the inscription's date is debated.
why: Writes Thai today.

sources.cite: Peter Daniels and William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Syriac
what: Aramaic script of Edessa.
why: Carried Christian texts as far as China; parent of Sogdian-era Central Asian scripts.

sources.cite: John Healey, Aramaic Inscriptions and Documents of the Roman Period (2009); Gruendler, The Development of the Arabic Scripts (1993)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Nabataean
what: Aramaic script of Petra.
why: The direct ancestor of Arabic.

sources.cite: John Healey, Aramaic Inscriptions and Documents of the Roman Period (2009); Gruendler, The Development of the Arabic Scripts (1993)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Arabic
what: Earliest dated texts in Arabic letters are from about 512.
why: Spread with Islam from Spain to Indonesia; second most used script.

sources.cite: John Healey, Aramaic Inscriptions and Documents of the Roman Period (2009); Gruendler, The Development of the Arabic Scripts (1993)
Michael Macdonald, "Ancient Arabia and the written word", in The Development of Arabic as a Written Language (2010)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Hebrew square script
what: The Aramaic script as Jews wrote it, replacing Paleo-Hebrew.
why: Script of the Dead Sea Scrolls and of Hebrew today.

sources.cite: Joseph Naveh, Early History of the Alphabet (1982)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Sogdian
what: Script of the Silk Road's merchant people.
why: Parent of Old Uyghur and so of Mongolian and Manchu.

sources.cite: Peter Daniels and William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Old Turkic (Orkhon)
what: Runic-looking letters on the steles of Bilge Khagan and Kül Tegin (732).
why: The first written Turkic.

sources.cite: Talât Tekin, A Grammar of Orkhon Turkic (1968)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Old Uyghur
what: Sogdian letters used for Turkic.
why: Parent of the Mongolian script.

sources.cite: Peter Daniels and William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Mongolian script
what: Adopted from Uyghur scribes under Chinggis Khan; written top to bottom.
why: Still used in Inner Mongolia.

sources.cite: Juha Janhunen (ed.), The Mongolic Languages (2003)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Coptic
what: Greek letters plus six from Demotic.
why: Last stage of written Egyptian.

sources.cite: Peter Daniels and William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Gothic
what: Made by bishop Wulfila to translate the Bible.
why: The oldest long text in a Germanic language.

sources.cite: Peter Daniels and William Bright (eds.), The World's Writing Systems (1996)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Runes (Elder Futhark)
what: Probably from a north Italic alphabet.
why: Germanic peoples' own script before Latin.

sources.cite: Tineke Looijenga, Texts and Contexts of the Oldest Runic Inscriptions (2003)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Ogham
what: Notches along the edge of a standing stone.
why: Oldest written Irish; built on the Latin letter scheme.

sources.cite: Damian McManus, A Guide to Ogam (1991)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Armenian
what: Invented by Mesrop Mashtots.
why: A Christian kingdom's own script, still used.

sources.cite: James Russell, "Alphabets (Armenian)", Encyclopaedia Iranica (1986); Gippert, "The Georgian script", in The Languages and Literatures of Georgia (2023)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Georgian
what: Oldest inscriptions from the 430s.
why: Still used; its origin story credits King Pharnavaz.

sources.cite: James Russell, "Alphabets (Armenian)", Encyclopaedia Iranica (1986); Gippert, "The Georgian script", in The Languages and Literatures of Georgia (2023)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Glagolitic
what: Created by Saint Cyril for the Moravian mission.
why: The first Slavic script.

sources.cite: Paul Cubberley, "The Slavic alphabets", in The World's Writing Systems (1996)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Cyrillic
what: Greek capitals plus Glagolitic letters, made in the First Bulgarian Empire.
why: Spread with Orthodox Christianity and later Soviet policy.

sources.cite: Paul Cubberley, "The Slavic alphabets", in The World's Writing Systems (1996)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Chinese characters
what: Oracle-bone inscriptions of the late Shang.
why: The oldest writing system still in use; adopted for Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese.

sources.cite: David Keightley, Sources of Shang History: The Oracle-Bone Inscriptions of Bronze Age China (1978)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Japanese kana
what: Simplified Chinese characters used for sound (man'yogana, then hiragana and katakana).
why: Let Japanese write its own grammar.

sources.cite: Christopher Seeley, A History of Writing in Japan (1991)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Hangul
what: Designed under King Sejong, announced 1446.
why: Letter shapes show how the mouth makes each sound; made so commoners could read.

sources.cite: Ki-Moon Lee and Robert Ramsey, A History of the Korean Language (2011)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Zapotec script
what: Carved stones from the Oaxaca valley.
why: One of the oldest Mesoamerican writings; mostly undeciphered.

sources.cite: Joyce Marcus, Mesoamerican Writing Systems (1992)

name: Maya script
what: Earliest securely dated glyphs at San Bartolo, about 300 BCE.
why: The only fully developed writing of the pre-Columbian Americas; deciphered after Knorozov (1952).

sources.cite: William Saturno, David Stuart and Boris Beltrán, "Early Maya writing at San Bartolo, Guatemala", Science 311 (2006)
Michael Coe, Breaking the Maya Code (1992)

name: Meroitic
what: Signs taken from Egyptian, used for Kush's own language.
why: Readable, but the language is barely understood.

sources.cite: Claude Rilly, La langue du royaume de Méroé (2007)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Libyco-Berber (Tifinagh)
what: Berber writing of Numidia; Tuareg Tifinagh descends from it.
why: Revived as Neo-Tifinagh for Amazigh in Morocco.

sources.cite: Werner Pichler, Origin and Development of the Libyco-Berber Script (2007)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Cherokee syllabary
what: Invented by Sequoyah, who could not read any other script.
why: Most Cherokee were literate within a few years.

sources.cite: Willard Walker and James Sarbaugh, "The early history of the Cherokee syllabary", Ethnohistory 40 (1993)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Vai syllabary
what: Credited to Momolu Duwalu Bukele.
why: Among the first scripts invented in sub-Saharan Africa still in use.

sources.cite: David Dalby, "A survey of the indigenous scripts of Liberia and Sierra Leone", African Language Studies 8 (1967)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Cree syllabics
what: Devised by missionary James Evans; the shape's turn gives the vowel.
why: Spread among Cree and Inuit faster than missionaries could.

sources.cite: John Murdoch, Syllabics: A Successful Educational Innovation (1981)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: N'Ko
what: Invented by Solomana Kanté for Manding languages.
why: An answer to claims that African languages could not be written.

sources.cite: Dianne Oyler, "A cultural revolution in Africa: literacy in the Republic of Guinea since independence", International Journal of African Historical Studies 34 (2001)
Unicode Consortium, ISO 15924 script codes

name: Rongorongo
what: Glyphs on wooden tablets.
why: Undeciphered; maybe invented after seeing Spanish writing in 1770.
